134.title: Walking in
134.hook: behind a screen or face to face; bless me Father, it's been this long
134.carry: the hardest part is the door
134.howItsDone: Catholics go to confession at set parish times, often Saturday afternoons, choosing to kneel behind a screen or sit face to face, and usually begin by saying how long it has been since their last confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, conscience, and a slow look back. Your line was look honestly, not harshly. How did the look back go last night? Day one hundred thirty-four.

Saturday afternoon, a side aisle of a parish church. Five people sit in a pew near a wooden door with a little light above it. When the light goes off, the next one gets up. You can tell who hasn't been in years: they're reading a card from the pamphlet rack, lips moving, and when it's their turn they stand up like someone going in for a job interview. Ask a priest who hears confessions and he may tell you the same thing. The hardest part isn't what's said inside. It's the walk from the pew to the door. Today: walking in.
screen: `A LIGHT ABOVE A WOODEN DOOR.` → `LIPS MOVING, READING A CARD.` → `THE WALK FROM THE PEW.`

segments.voice: Let's take the mystery out of it. First, the room. For long stretches of Church history there was no box. People confessed face to face, often kneeling beside the priest. Historians link the wooden confessional with a screen to the years after the Council of Trent, and to Charles Borromeo, archbishop of Milan, who promoted it to protect privacy and dignity. Today, many parishes offer both. You can kneel behind the screen and stay anonymous, or sit in a chair across from the priest. It's your choice, and nobody minds which. Then, the words. There's a traditional opening: Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. Then you say how long it's been since your last confession. A week. Two years. Twenty-five years. Priests hear every answer, and a long time is not a scandal; it's a return. If you've forgotten what to do, you can simply say so. The priest will walk you through it. That's part of his job. Then you say your sins, simply, without a speech. Serious ones should be named with roughly how often; you don't need to tell the whole backstory. The priest may give a few words of advice, or read a short line of Scripture. After that comes a prayer of sorrow, a penance, and the words of absolution, which are the next two days. And if you truly can't remember something, the Church teaches it's forgiven along with the rest, as long as it wasn't hidden on purpose. The whole thing is often over in a few minutes. The door is the hard part.
screen: `NO BOX FOR MOST OF HISTORY.` · `BEHIND A SCREEN, OR FACE TO FACE.` · `BLESS ME, FATHER, FOR I HAVE SINNED.` · `SAY IT SIMPLY. HE'LL HELP.` · then, large: `THE HARDEST PART IS THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn the opening words. Settle, and breathe. If you're Catholic, say them quietly to yourself: Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been, and then however long it's really been. Notice how that feels to say. If you're not Catholic, think of a door you've been avoiding: an apology, a doctor's appointment, a conversation. Picture yourself walking up to it. Standing there. Opening it. That's all. The bell holds the time.
Walking in. Behind a screen or face to face, with the old opening words, bless me, Father, and however long it's been. Today's word.
Your line: the hardest part is the door. Today, walk through one small door you've been putting off, and notice how much lighter the room is on the other side. Day one hundred thirty-four.

135.title: The act of contrition
135.hook: sorry because of love, not only fear, and a promise to try again
135.howItsDone: Near the end of confession Catholics pray an act of contrition, often the traditional one learned as children, or in their own words, and some also pray one each night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking in, from the pew to the confessional door. Your line was the hardest part is the door. Which small door did you walk through? Day one hundred thirty-five.

Two kids break a neighbor's window with a baseball. The first one says sorry because his dad is standing right there with that look. The second one says sorry because she likes the old man next door, and she can see his face at the broken window, and it hurts her that she did that to him. Both apologies count. But they aren't the same. One is sorry about getting caught. The other is sorry about the person. Catholics have an old word for this, and a prayer to go with it. Today: contrition.
screen: `TWO KIDS, ONE WINDOW.` → `SORRY ABOUT GETTING CAUGHT.` → `SORRY ABOUT THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Contrition comes from the Latin conterere, to grind down, to crush, like grain between stones. A contrite heart is one that's been broken open. The Psalms use the picture: in the Douay-Rheims, "a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." Catholic teaching names two kinds of sorrow, a lot like those two kids. The first is sorrow out of love for God, because sin hurts someone who is good. That's called perfect contrition. The second is sorrow because of what sin does: its ugliness, or fear of its consequences. That's called imperfect contrition, or attrition. Here's the merciful part: the Church teaches that imperfect sorrow is enough to begin with, inside the sacrament. You don't have to feel exactly the right thing before you walk in. Near the end of confession, the penitent says an act of contrition. One traditional version begins: "O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended thee." It goes on to name both kinds of sorrow, fear and love, and ends with a firm resolve, with God's help, to sin no more and to avoid what leads to it. That resolve matters. Sorrow without it is only a feeling. Sorrow with it becomes a turn. But you don't have to use the memorized version. The Church allows an act of contrition in your own words, as long as it says you're sorry and you mean to try again. Look at Peter after he denied Jesus three times. The Douay-Rheims says simply: "And Peter going out, wept bitterly." He didn't give up. He came back.
screen: `CONTERERE: TO GRIND, TO CRUSH.` · `SORRY FROM LOVE, OR FROM FEAR.` · `O MY GOD, I AM HEARTILY SORRY.` · `IN YOUR OWN WORDS IS FINE.` · then, large: `SORRY, AND RESOLVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: an act of contrition in your own words. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the one thing from your look back two days ago, or something new. Now ask: who did it hurt? Picture their face. Let the sorry be about them, not about how you look. Then find one small thing you'll do differently. If you pray, you can tell God both, in your own words, as simple as you like. If you don't, just say them to yourself: I'm sorry, and I'll try. The bell holds the time.
Contrition. From the Latin for crushed. Sorrow for sin, best when it comes from love, always joined to a promise to try again. Today's word.
Your line: sorry, and resolved. Today, if you owe someone an apology, make it about them, and add one thing you'll do differently. Day one hundred thirty-five.

136.title: Absolution and penance
136.hook: I absolve you, and a small penance to begin the repair
136.howItsDone: At the end of confession the priest extends his hand and says the words of absolution; the penitent answers amen and later does the penance he gave, often a few prayers or a small act of repair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, contrition: sorry from love, not only fear. Your line was sorry, and resolved. Did you make an apology about the other person? Day one hundred thirty-six.

A hiker carries a heavy pack for so long she forgets it's there. She just walks a little bent over. Then someone lifts it off her shoulders, and for a second she nearly floats. Some people who come out of confession after years away describe it like that. They sit in the pew afterward, a bit stunned, lighter. What happened in there came down to a few words spoken by a priest, and then a small job to do on the way out. Today: absolution, and penance.
screen: `A PACK SHE FORGOT.` → `LIFTED OFF.` → `A FEW WORDS, AND A SMALL JOB.`

segments.voice: Absolution comes from the Latin absolvere, to loosen, to set free, to untie. It's the same root as absolute and solve. When the priest absolves, Catholics believe the knots are untied. After the penitent's act of contrition, the priest extends his hand over their head and prays a short prayer of absolution. It names God as the Father of mercies who reconciled the world through the death and resurrection of his Son and sent the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins. And it ends with the words that are the heart of the sacrament. In the old Latin form: Ego te absolvo a peccatis tuis, in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti. I absolve you from your sins, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The penitent answers amen. Catholics believe every sin confessed with real sorrow is forgiven then and there, completely. But there's one more piece, and it's often misunderstood: the penance. The priest gives a small task, often a few prayers, sometimes an act of kindness, reading a passage, or making something right. It isn't payment. You can't buy forgiveness, and the Church says so. It's more like physical therapy after surgery. The sin is forgiven, but it has left some damage, in you and around you, and penance begins the repair. When you can, repair means real repair: returning what was taken, fixing what was broken. Zacchaeus, the tax collector, shows it. In the Douay-Rheims, he says to Jesus: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have wronged any man of any thing, I restore him fourfold." Forgiven, and then sent out to mend.
screen: `ABSOLVERE: TO LOOSEN, TO UNTIE.` · `EGO TE ABSOLVO.` · `PENANCE ISN'T PAYMENT.` · `ZACCHAEUS RESTORES FOURFOLD.` · then, large: `FORGIVEN, THEN SENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one act of repair. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the things you've looked at this week. Is there something you damaged, even a little? A trust, a friendship, a borrowed thing, a reputation you shaded in conversation. Pick one. Now choose one small, concrete act that begins to fix it. A call. A correction. Giving something back. Keep it doable today. If you pray, you can ask for help to do it well. The bell holds the time.
Absolution. From the Latin for untying. The priest's words of forgiveness, and after them, a small penance to begin the repair. Today's word.
Your line: forgiven, then sent. Today, do the one act of repair you chose, and don't wait for the perfect moment. Day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: The seal
137.hook: a priest may never reveal what he hears, under any pressure (CCC 1467)
137.tomorrow: The tabernacle and the red lamp
137.howItsDone: Catholics confess trusting that the priest is bound by the seal: he may never reveal or use what he hears, and a priest who directly breaks it is automatically excommunicated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, absolution: untied, and then a penance to begin the repair. Your line was forgiven, then sent. Did you do your act of repair? Day one hundred thirty-seven.

Everyone knows what it's like to tell a secret and then watch it travel. You tell one friend, and within a week three people look at you differently. So here's a question worth sitting with. Why would anyone walk into a small room and tell a stranger the worst things they've done? Part of the answer is a promise the Catholic Church makes, one of the strictest promises of silence in the world. The priest who hears you will carry it to his grave. Today: the seal of confession.
screen: `A SECRET THAT TRAVELS.` → `WHY TELL A STRANGER?` → `CARRIED TO THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: The seal is called a seal because it's meant to be closed like a sealed letter, the old kind with wax and a signet ring, never to be opened. The Latin word is sigillum. The Catechism, in paragraph 1467, says a priest who hears confessions is bound to absolute secrecy about the sins confessed to him, with no exceptions. Church law calls the seal inviolable. A priest may not reveal a penitent's sins by word, by hint, or in any other way, to anyone, ever. Not to the police, not to a court, not to the penitent's family, not even to the penitent later, unless the penitent brings it up. He can't even use what he heard to change how he treats someone. A priest who directly breaks the seal is automatically excommunicated. And it binds others too: an interpreter, or anyone who overhears, must also keep it. Why so strict? Because the whole sacrament depends on it. If people couldn't trust the silence, they wouldn't come, and the door to forgiveness would close. Catholics tell the story of John of Nepomuk, a priest in Prague in 1393, drowned in the river on the orders of King Wenceslaus the Fourth. Tradition says the king wanted to know what his queen had confessed, and John refused. Historians debate the details, but he's honored as a martyr of the seal. In our own time, some governments have tried to require priests to report certain things heard in confession. The Church's answer hasn't changed: the seal can't be broken. That doesn't mean a priest does nothing. He can urge a penitent to turn themselves in or to get help, but he can't speak.
screen: `SIGILLUM: A SEAL ON A LETTER.` · `NO EXCEPTIONS, EVER.` · `WHY: SO PEOPLE CAN COME.` · `JOHN OF NEPOMUK, PRAGUE, 1393.` · then, large: `WHAT'S SAID THERE STAYS THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one secret faithfully. Settle, and breathe. Think of something someone has told you in confidence. A worry, a mistake, a hope they aren't ready to share. Picture their face as they told you. Notice the trust in that moment. Now decide, quietly, that it stays with you. Not a hint, not a knowing look, not a someone told me. If you pray, you can pray for that person without naming what they said. The bell holds the time.
Seal of confession. The absolute silence a priest keeps about what he hears, with no exceptions, so that anyone can come. Today's word.

Your line: what's said there stays there. That's confession, up close: conscience, walking in, contrition, absolution, the seal. Today, keep one confidence completely. Tomorrow, a red lamp in the dark. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

138.title: The tabernacle and the red lamp
138.hook: the lamp burning beside it tells you the Eucharist is reserved there
138.howItsDone: Catholics genuflect toward the tabernacle when they enter or pass it, and many stop in a church during the day to pray quietly near the sanctuary lamp.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seal of confession, the silence that lets anyone come. Your line was what's said there stays there. Did you keep a confidence completely? Day one hundred thirty-eight.

A Catholic church on a weekday afternoon. It's quiet. Maybe an older man in the back pew, maybe nobody at all. The lights are low. And somewhere near the front, usually to one side, there's a small flame in a red glass, burning steadily. It burns all night when the doors are locked. It burns on holidays. If you drove past a house and saw a light on in the window at three in the morning, you'd think: someone's home. Catholics mean something like that. Today's word: tabernacle.
screen: `A QUIET CHURCH, A WEEKDAY.` → `A SMALL FLAME IN RED GLASS.` → `A LIGHT ON IN THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: The flame is the sanctuary lamp, and it burns beside the tabernacle, a small, locked box, often gold, sometimes a little house of carved wood or stone. Inside are consecrated hosts left over from Mass. Catholics believe Jesus is truly present in them, so the tabernacle is kept with great honor. Church law says a special lamp should burn before it at all times, to show and honor that presence. Red is the usual custom. So the lamp is a sign you can read from the door: if it's lit, the Eucharist is reserved here. That's why Catholics genuflect, bending the right knee to the floor, when they pass the tabernacle. Why keep hosts at all? First, for the sick and dying: the Catechism says the Eucharist was first reserved so it could be carried to those who couldn't come to Mass. Over time, people also began to come and pray before it. Now the word. Tabernacle comes from the Latin tabernaculum, a tent. In the book of Exodus, while Israel wandered in the desert, God asked for a tent to be made so he could live among the people. In the Douay-Rheims: "And they shall make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in the midst of them." That tent was the tabernacle, and a lamp burned in it too. John's Gospel picks up the same image: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." In Greek, dwelt literally means pitched his tent. So the little box in the church carries a long story: God wanting to live next door, in a tent, among his people.
screen: `A LOCKED BOX, A LAMP BESIDE IT.` · `IF IT'S LIT, THE HOST IS KEPT HERE.` · `TABERNACULUM: A TENT.` · `THE WORD PITCHED HIS TENT.` · then, large: `I WILL DWELL IN THE MIDST OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the red lamp. Right now, picture a church you know, and try to remember where its lamp is. If you can't, that's your task this week: walk in and look for it. For now, settle, and breathe. Imagine sitting in that quiet church near the flame. You don't have to say anything. If you pray, you can simply say hello, the way you would to someone home. If you don't, just notice what it's like to sit near a light that never goes out. The bell holds the time.
Tabernacle. From the Latin for a tent. The place in a church where the Eucharist is kept, with a lamp burning beside it. Today's word.
Your line: someone is home. Today, when you pass a church, look for a sign of life, and give it a nod. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

139.title: The monstrance
139.hook: a gold sunburst that shows the host so people can pray before it
139.tomorrow: Could you not watch one hour (Matthew 26:40)
139.howItsDone: In Eucharistic adoration a priest or deacon places a consecrated host in a monstrance on the altar, and Catholics come to sit or kneel before it in silent prayer, sometimes for an hour, sometimes around the clock.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tabernacle, and the red lamp beside it. Your line was someone is home. Did you look for a light in a church? Day one hundred thirty-nine.

There's a story from a small French village in the 1800s. The parish priest, John Vianney, kept noticing an old farmer who came into the church every day and sat for a long time in front of the tabernacle. He never seemed to move his lips. No beads, no book. Finally the priest asked him what he said to God all that time. The farmer answered, more or less: nothing. I look at him, and he looks at me. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it. And there's an object built for exactly that kind of looking. Today: the monstrance.
screen: `A FRENCH VILLAGE, THE 1800S.` → `NO BEADS, NO BOOK.` → `I LOOK AT HIM. HE LOOKS AT ME.`

segments.voice: Monstrance comes from the Latin monstrare, to show. It's the same root as demonstrate. A monstrance is a holder, usually gold, with a small round window of glass in the center. A single consecrated host is placed behind the glass, so people can see it. Around that window, very often, are golden rays bursting out in every direction like a sun. Some are simple; some are covered in jewels and taller than a child. The host is the point; the rest is a frame. Why build such a thing? Historians describe a medieval longing to see the host; in that period the priest began lifting it high at Mass, so everyone could look. In 1264 the feast of Corpus Christi, the Body of Christ, was extended to the whole Church, with processions carrying the Eucharist through the streets. People wanted to see it outside of Mass too, and the monstrance grew out of that desire. When the host is placed in a monstrance on the altar, it's called exposition. People come and pray before it, and this is called adoration. Catholics believe they are looking at Jesus himself. Behind it is a plain idea: prayer doesn't have to be words. You don't need to perform, or produce anything, or get it right. You can simply sit and look, and let yourself be looked at, like the old farmer.
screen: `MONSTRARE: TO SHOW.` · `A HOST BEHIND GLASS, A GOLD SUN.` · `A MEDIEVAL LONGING TO SEE.` · `PRAYER WITHOUT WORDS.` · then, large: `I LOOK AT HIM, AND HE LOOKS AT ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one thing for the whole sit. Settle, and breathe. Choose something near you: a candle, a tree outside the window, a cup, a photograph of someone you love. Rest your eyes on it. Don't analyze it. Don't narrate it in your head. When your mind wanders, bring your eyes back, gently. If you pray, you can let this looking be your prayer, with no words at all. If you don't, just practice seeing one thing fully. The bell holds the time.
Monstrance. From the Latin for showing. The gold holder, often a sunburst, that shows the host so people can pray just by looking. Today's word.
Your line: just looking is prayer. Today, look at one person you love for a moment longer than usual, without saying anything. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

140.title: Could you not watch one hour (Matthew 26:40)
140.hook: a holy hour answers his question in Gethsemane
140.howItsDone: Some Catholics make a holy hour, an hour of prayer before the Eucharist in a church or adoration chapel, often weekly on a set day, and some parishes keep adoration around the clock with sign-up hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monstrance, the gold frame that shows the host. Your line was just looking is prayer. Who did you look at a moment longer? Day one hundred forty.

It's late at night in a garden of olive trees outside Jerusalem. Jesus has brought his three closest friends, Peter, James and John, and asked them one thing: stay awake with me. Then he goes a little way off, falls on his face, and prays in anguish. When he comes back, they're asleep. Staying up with a sick child or a grieving friend goes like that. The eyes just close. And Jesus says something to Peter that the Church still repeats. Today: the holy hour.

segments.voice: Here's what he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" Some readers hear no anger in it, only disappointment, even tenderness. He goes on: watch ye, and pray, that ye enter not into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. The Greek word for watch there is gregoreo: stay awake, keep alert, be on guard. The name Gregory is usually traced to the same root: the watchful one. Catholics who keep a holy hour see it as answering that question with a yes. A holy hour is exactly what it sounds like: an hour spent in prayer, usually before the Eucharist in a church or chapel, often in adoration before the monstrance. Its modern form is often traced to Margaret Mary Alacoque, a French nun in the 1670s, who said Jesus asked her to spend an hour on Thursday nights keeping him company in his agony. The practice spread. Fulton Sheen, the American bishop famous on early television, made a holy hour every day of his priesthood and said it was the secret of whatever good he did. Some parishes now have adoration chapels where someone signs up for each hour, so that day and night, someone is always watching. What do you do for an hour? Pray, read Scripture, say a rosary, write, sit in silence, or simply look, like yesterday's farmer. Some who keep the hour say the start is the hardest, and then something settles. And if an hour is too much, Catholics would say: start with less. The point is to stay awake with him.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit without your phone. Put it in another room, or face down, out of reach. Settle, and breathe. For the time the bell gives you, do nothing else. Just stay awake, and stay here. Notice how many times your hand wants to reach for something. Let it rest. If you pray, you can think of Jesus in the garden and simply keep him company. If you don't, keep company with the quiet. Later today, try five minutes. The bell holds the time.
